title: Kemi Badenoch says Tories would scrap inheritance tax on family homes
description: Rival parties hit back and said the proposals for IHT, which is levied on the value of someone's estate when they die, would prioritise support for we
body: Rival parties hit back and said the proposals for IHT, which is levied on the value of someone's estate when they die, would prioritise support for wealthier people in the country.Badenoch arrived in Birmingham's Symphony Hall with a message to Conservative Party members that they face a "battle for the soul of the this nation".She argued her party is "renewed" and "coming back" as she continued efforts to convince voters that it has changed following an historic defeat at the 2024 general election.In a nod to those who have defected to Nigel Farage's party, Badenoch said: "The Conservatives have had an export boom of drama queens going to Reform. "This party is now the no drama party, we are the no-nonsense party."With the party trailing Labour and Reform in the polls, Badenoch acknowledged that people are "looking through the shop window", they "like what they see" but "not enough of them are buying yet, we need to fix that".Her inspiration for how to revive a long-standing brand was Marks and Spencer (M&S), saying they have "adapted their style for today's market and people are flooding back".Badenoch added: "Just like M&S, we must learn from our mistakes, win back trust and make people feel good about our party again."One of the biggest responses in the room from members came as Badenoch made clear she did not want to do an election deal with Reform.She described many Reform voters as "our people", adding: "We let them down and we want them to come back home."Following a section of the speech mocking some of Reform's senior figures, Badenoch said: "To those who say 'unite the right', we are not uniting with that."People deserve better than that and we are going to give them better than that. Character, conduct, and standards matter."She also said she did not want to live in a country run by people who "debate whether my mixed-race children are English".In one of many jibes aimed at Burnham, Badenoch labelled him a "Paddington Bear prime minister" who was "hoping that the problems will just go away".In the days ahead of Wednesday's speech, there was widespread speculation that Badenoch would announce changes to IHT.As the opposition leader neared the end of her 66-minute speech, she said IHT was "supposed to be a tax on the super wealthy" but it is "now a tax on ordinary middle-class families in every corner of our country".She said: "The next Conservative government will legislate so nobody will ever pay inheritance tax on their family home."On top of that, couples would be able to leave an additional £1m tax-free and these changes mean every inheritance tax bill will be cut and the number of families paying inheritance tax will fall by more than half."The Conservatives have estimated the policy would cost around £6bn a year and believe they have identified £71bn of savings that can be made to government spending, including welfare cuts.Under the current rules, estates worth more than £325,000, or £500,000 if a home is left to children or grandchildren, can face a 40% tax rate on assets above the threshold.Married or civil partners can also transfer assets between each other.In 2023-24, 4.72% of UK deaths resulted in an IHT charge and raised around £7bn for the government.Badenoch also said her "ambition is to abolish inheritance tax altogether, as soon as we can afford it".Labour Party chairwoman Bridget Phillipson said: "The Tories haven't changed. "Kemi Badenoch has shown that the Tories' choice is to do nothing to help ordinary families struggling with the cost of social care, prioritising the wealthiest instead."Reform UK economy spokesman Robert Jenrick said Badenoch had "chickened out of doing anything big" and is "for the 2%".The former Tory MP said: "While the Tory Party is offering handouts to multi-millionaires, Reform will give everyone a £500 tax cut by raising the tax-free personal allowance to £15,000. "The Tory Party is looking after its own in Kensington, Reform is looking after the country."Elsewhere in her speech, Badenoch referred to other policies the party has announced in recent days.These include a £10bn anti-missile defence system, 50,000 new prison places and halving the rate of employer national insurance on earnings for people aged between 21 to 24.They also pledged to scrap the "cliff edge" that means parents in England lose out on childcare support when they earn more than £100,000 a year.Another policy to be scrapped would be the High Value Council Tax Surcharge (HVCTS), dubbed the "mansion tax". This is due to take effect from 2028 and introduces an extra levy for owners of properties in England valued at more than £2m.Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey responded to the speech by saying Badenoch had been "lecturing the country on fiscal responsibility while making tens of billions in unfunded promises".Green MP Carla Denyer added: "Kemi Badenoch once again defined the Conservative Party as pro-billionaires, pro-inequality and pro-damaging the environment."

schema.headline: Kemi Badenoch says Tories would scrap inheritance tax on family homes

title: We spent thousands on a Tui river cruise but ended up on coach trips
description: David Mallon and a group of five others were due to travel on 21 September. But they decided the new itinerary presented to them a few days before dep
body: David Mallon and a group of five others were due to travel on 21 September. But they decided the new itinerary presented to them a few days before departure was so different from what they had booked that they didn't want to go."What they were planning to give us was not a cruise but a glorified coach trip," says David.One reason for not wanting to accept the new plan was that a member of the group was meant to be avoiding long periods of sitting down - such as coach journeys - for health reasons.With no offer of a refund, the group booked a last-minute holiday to Kos instead and decided to try and claim money back on their return."We don't blame Tui for the water levels, but it's the way they've handled the consequences of that," David says.He has now submitted a complaint to Tui and says he will take his quest for a refund to the small claims court if necessary. The BBC contacted Tui River Cruises about passengers' unhappiness with the extensive itinerary changes and the fact they were not offered any refund.  In a statement, a spokesperson said: "Extreme heat across Europe this summer caused low water levels on the Danube, affecting river cruise operators across the region. We review every sailing individually with our nautical partners."Customers on the Tui Isla departures on 14 and 21 September were sent revised itineraries before travelling. Where the ship couldn't sail sections of the river, we arranged coach transfers, hotel stays and adjusted travel arrangements to minimise transfer times so customers could still visit destinations, including Budapest, Vienna and Bratislava."We reviewed the revised arrangements carefully and customers continued their holiday on the amended itinerary under our standard booking conditions. While customers were still able to visit the key destinations on their itinerary, we're sorry some did not get the river cruise experience they had anticipated."

schema.headline: We spent thousands on a Tui river cruise but ended up on coach trips

title: Harmanpreet Kaur: India's trailblazing women's cricket captain steps down
description: When Harmanpreet Kaur scored that unforgettable World Cup century against Australia in the 2017 semi-final, she not only changed the course of a match
body: When Harmanpreet Kaur scored that unforgettable World Cup century against Australia in the 2017 semi-final, she not only changed the course of a match but the trajectory of women's cricket in India. India went on to lose the final to England that year but women's cricket no longer remained a passing pursuit for the average Indian fan.    That dogged zeal to win she infused into the team helped them lift India's first women's World Cup trophy - the same feat that had eluded them in 2017 - in emphatic fashion eight years later.  Less than a year on, and within weeks of victories in the Asia Cup and the Asian Games, she has relinquished the captaincy, ending an era in which she became the team's most influential leader and one of the most recognisable figures in the sport.Star opener Smriti Mandhana, her long-time deputy, has been appointed captain across all formats.Board of Control for Cricket in India (BCCI) secretary Devajit Saikia, coach Amol Muzumdar, Harmanpreet and Mandhana attended the review meeting at which the leadership change was ratified. The transition, however, was not entirely seamless.Reports suggest the 37-year-old Harmanpreet was willing to relinquish the T20 captaincy immediately, but was keen to continue leading the side in One-Day Internationals and Tests so that younger players could benefit from her experience.The BCCI, however, was intent on a younger person at the helm and opted for the 30-year-old Mandhana.In some ways, the move mirrors the BCCI's decision to replace Suryakumar Yadav as captain of the men's T20 side shortly after India won the World Cup earlier this year, with the captaincy passing to Shreyas Iyer.Harmanpreet's future as captain had become a subject of intense debate in cricketing circles after India's below-par performance at the T20 World Cup in England a few months ago.Her own poor form with the bat amplified concerns and prompted the BCCI to consider changes that could help the team meet the growing challenges of a women's game that continues to expand rapidly around the world.Approaching her 38th birthday, and after almost a decade at the helm, Harmanpreet found herself under increasing scrutiny as her form dipped.Opinion on whether she should continue as captain was sharply divided among former women players and captains.Former cricketer Diana Edulji, among the most respected names in the game, felt Harmanpreet had done everything that could reasonably have been expected of her and that it was time for a younger captain to take over. Former captain Anjum Chopra, meanwhile, argued that Harmanpreet's experience remained invaluable and that she should stay on.Sensing that the BCCI was strongly inclined towards a change, Harmanpreet opted to step down during the review meeting. She later announced her decision in an emotional Instagram post."I feel I have done my duty. I gave this team everything I had," she wrote."Now, it is time for me to turn the page… Blood. Sweat. Sacrifice. Pride. I gave it all. Now, I'm ready to play for the love of the game again."Captaincy ends, the journey continues."Harmanpreet's intention to continue playing now leaves the BCCI with another decision to make about her future.In Suryakumar Yadav's case, he not only lost the captaincy but also his place in India's T20 side. Given the depth of talent available in the men's game, it was easier for Ajit Agarkar and his fellow selectors to take what was always likely to be a contentious decision.The situation in the women's game is different. Despite Harmanpreet's modest recent form, replacing a player of her experience and stature may not be straightforward, as the talent pipeline is not yet as deep as it is in men's cricket.Whatever the future holds, Harmanpreet has scripted among the more memorable careers in women's cricket. Spanning more than two decades, it is a journey marked by significant achievements and milestones.Born into a family of modest means in Punjab's Moga city, Harmanpreet developed a passion for cricket at an early age.Her family's support was vital in the early years, but her rise to national recognition came after she joined the Railways - a transition facilitated by Diana Edulji - and moved to Mumbai.The superior facilities and greater professionalism associated with Mumbai's sporting culture helped accelerate her development. She made her India debut in 2009 at the age of 20 and has remained an integral part of the national side across formats ever since.An all-rounder for the better part of her first decade in cricket, she made herself indispensable to the side with her explosive middle-order batting, crafty off-spin and sharp fielding skills.Her blistering century against Australia in the semi-final of the 2017 Women's ODI World Cup remains one of the defining knocks in the history of the women's game. India went on to lose to England in the final, but beating Australia was a monumental hurdle overcome.That century also helped spark wider interest in women's cricket in India, and transformed Harmanpreet into a household name.The second decade of her career showcased her prowess both as batter and captain. Having succeeded Mithali Raj as T20 captain in 2016, Harmanpreet assumed charge across all formats in 2022 and went on to guide India to some of the greatest successes in its history.Her leadership was marked by an aggressive pursuit of victory. That fearless approach instilled confidence and ambition in her teammates, helping the team overcome even the previously unbeatable Australians, most memorably in the semi-final of the 2025 ODI World Cup.Unlike in 2017, Harmanpreet couldn't get a hundred on that occasion, but her innings of 89 as was a stellar effort as captain. Combined with Jemimah Rodrigues's century, it helped India secure a famous victory over their arch rivals. India then defeated South Africa in the final to reach what many regard as the pinnacle of achievement in the history of Indian women's cricket.With multiple titles and trophies won under her leadership, Harmanpreet leaves behind a formidable legacy for her successor, Smriti Mandhana, to emulate.

schema.headline: Harmanpreet Kaur: India's trailblazing women's cricket captain steps down

title: World's largest penguin colony hit by climate-driven decline
description: World's largest penguin colony hit by 'alarming' decline in numbersImage source, British Antarctic SurveyImage caption, Chinstrap penguins get their n
body: World's largest penguin colony hit by 'alarming' decline in numbersImage source, British Antarctic SurveyImage caption, Chinstrap penguins get their name from a thin ring of feathers from ear to earByVictoria GillScience CorrespondentAlmost two-thirds of the population of chinstrap penguins have disappeared from a remote volcanic island near Antarctica, aerial surveys suggest.Zavodovski Island was home to the largest penguin colony in the world, but researchers who carried out the surveys say it has now lost that accolade. According to the study, there were 63% fewer occupied nests of chinstrap penguins in 2025 than at the same time in 2011.The research team say climate change is affecting the birds' food supply and survival, and the penguins may now be officially endangered.Another species of penguin, the macaroni, also nests on the island and is thriving, which scientists believe is linked to their more varied diet.Image source, British Antarctic SurveyImage caption, The scientists used drones and trackers to study the penguin colonyZavodovski is part of the South Sandwich Islands, a remote archipelago north of the Antarctic continent which is a UK overseas territory. In 2011, it was hailed by the British Antarctic Survey (BAS) as home to the largest penguin colony in the world - with an estimated 600,000 chinstrap penguins and 90,000 macaroni penguins nesting on its bleak, rocky terrain. BAS, which led this new research, says it is "one of the most extreme places in the world to undertake fieldwork".A BAS team sailed for 15 days to reach the island and study its avian inhabitants, using drones, aerial photography and fitting tracking devices to 20 birds. This research and satellite imagery suggested that - between 2011 and 2025 - the number of occupied chinstrap penguin nests declined by 63%.Where did all the penguins go? Image source, British Antarctic SurveyImage caption, Macaroni penguin populations increased as chinstrap penguins declinedThe researchers say the "alarming" fall in the chinstrap population is all about the food supply and rising ocean temperatures brought about by climate change. Prof Norman Ratcliffe, who led the research, explained that the chinstraps' "specialist diet" and preference for cooler waters appears to have left them vulnerable."With waters warming, the krill [that the chinstrap penguins eat] have moved southwards. "Sea-ice cover to the south and a lack of suitable islands for nesting prevents chinstraps from following the food," he said.Hungry whales and active volcanoesThe team examined other possible threats to the penguins' precarious existence on their remote island. Birds here nest in the shadow of an active volcano - Mount Curry, also aptly known as Mount Asphyxsia.Sites downwind of the volcano have been given names including Stench Point, Noxious Bluff and Asphyxia Plain, because of the smell of fumes emitted from the crater.Dr Ratcliffe told BBC News: "When you add all the penguin guano on top of that, and you really do have one of the smelliest places in the world. "It's like a penguin Mordor."Mount Curry's last major eruption was back in 2016, but the penguin declines that this study analysed have been steady and ongoing since 2011, suggesting that something else was happening. Another concern was competition for the krill that chinstrap penguins rely on - possibly from migrating humpback whales. But, while the humpbacks eat huge quantities of krill, they also help boost krill production by fertilising marine plants that the krill feed on (with their huge quantities of whale poo). Researchers say a more fundamental, climate-driven shift in ocean food supplies is to blame. Image source, British Antarctic SurveyImage caption, Two chinstrap penguins on Zavodovski IslandThere is an unexpected element of this story that also adds to the picture of how - and why - this region is changing: While the chinstrap population has been declining, the number of macaroni penguins on the island has increased dramatically. Macaroni penguins, scientists say, are more adaptable, because they have a broader, more flexible diet. Tracking data from the study showed that the macaronis foraged in warmer waters to the northeast of the island, where scientists say they were were likely to be supplementing their diets with fish and other crustaceans. Dr Ratcliffe said this shift was "biggest change in community composition ever observed at a single location in Antarctica". "Our data shows that the cold-adapted Antarctic chinstrap species are no longer thriving beside their sub-Antarctic neighbours," he added. "It is further evidence of how rapid warming in the Antarctic is impacting unique and sensitive ecosystems."As for the title of world's largest penguin colony, scientists say that is now held by a site more than 5,000km away - on the other side of the Antarctic continent - Cape Adare in the Ross Sea.The research is published in the journal Current Biology, external. Image source, British Antarctic SurveyImage caption, Zavodovski's penguins nest in the shadow of an active volcano

schema.headline: World's largest penguin colony hit by climate-driven decline

title: Bank of England reveals the four animals to feature on banknotes
description: Hedgehog among four chosen animals to feature on your new banknotesImage source, Bank of England/PA WireByCost of living correspondentBanknotes are ge
body: Hedgehog among four chosen animals to feature on your new banknotesImage source, Bank of England/PA WireByCost of living correspondentBanknotes are getting a nature makeover - and the Bank of England has revealed the four creatures that will feature on our money.The Atlantic puffin, barn owl, buff-tailed bumblebee and European hedgehog will appear on the redesigned notes in years to come - although no decision has been made about which animal will be shown on which banknote.The owl, bumblebee and hedgehog topped a public vote in their specific categories, and the puffin was included to celebrate marine life, the coastline and bring variety to the notes, the Bank said.Wildlife is replacing notable figures from history, such as Sir Winston Churchill, on our cash in a decision that angered a number of leading politicians.  'Four distinct and inspiring animals'"We have chosen four distinct and inspiring animals that not only showcase the great variety of wildlife we have in the UK but will also enhance the security of our banknotes," said Victoria Cleland, the Bank's chief cashier.A panel of wildlife experts drew up a shortlist of 18 mammals, birds, amphibians insects and fish which were put forward to public nominations. Respondents were invited to select up to six.More than 2.5 million votes were cast by 478,531 people, ranging from wildlife enthusiasts to primary school classes. The buff-tailed bumblebee (Bombus terrestris) was a clear winner, receiving 360,399 votes, nearly 90,000 more than the barn owl (Tyto alba).The European hedgehog (Erinaceus europaeus) was most popular in the mammals category.The red fox, in the mammals category, and the common kingfisher, among the birds, received more nominations than the Atlantic puffin. The puffin (Fratercula arctica) was still selected because it was the most popular marine animal. The Bank said its inclusion added variety to the series, made the denominations easier to distinguish, and gave an opportunity to celebrate the British coastline.The puffin and bees also feature on coins, as part of the Royal Mint's redesigned 20p and £1 coins respectively. Image source, Bank of England/PA WireImage caption, Mock-ups of the new Bank of England banknotes featuring all four winners  Each of the quartet of creatures will feature as the central image of a £5, £10, £20 or £50 note, which will also feature other elements from nature as part of their designs, potentially including other shortlisted animals. The monarch will still feature on the other side of the notes.Rhys Phillips, the Bank's incoming chief cashier who will be responsible for the roll-out of the new series of notes, said the process of designing, testing and printing banknotes could take years.He said the Bank needed to make sure they were high-quality, resilient and accessible. As the designs were only in the very early stages, they would be unveiled closer to their launch."We'll now work to design, test and produce the banknotes, combining the imagery we've announced today with cutting-edge security features and materials science," he said.Wildlife already appears on banknotes in the UK, with mackerel, otters, red squirrels and osprey featuring on notes issued by the Royal Bank of Scotland, external.Figure caption, Churchill's granddaughter happy with his picture being replaced on the £5 noteYet it will be the first time since 1970 that the reverse side of Bank of England notes will no longer feature notable figures from history.On notes circulating currently, in ascending order of value, are former Prime Minister Sir Winston Churchill, author Jane Austen, artist JMW Turner and mathematician and wartime codebreaker Alan Turing.The proposed removal of wartime leader Churchill angered Reform leader Nigel Farage, and Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey, with Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch describing the move as "a silly thing to do".The Bank said the move was primarily to stop counterfeiting so all images needed to be replaced on banknotes over time.

schema.headline: Bank of England reveals the four animals to feature on banknotes

title: BBC's Nicky Campbell tells court teacher who attacked him 'completely lost it'
description: Image source, PA MediaImage caption, BBC presenter Nicky Campbell has been giving evidence about alleged abuse at Edinburgh AcademyBySteven GoddenBBC
body: Image source, PA MediaImage caption, BBC presenter Nicky Campbell has been giving evidence about alleged abuse at Edinburgh AcademyBySteven GoddenBBC ScotlandUpdated 5 hours agoBroadcaster Nicky Campbell has told a court a maths teacher "completely lost it" and violently attacked him in the courtyard of Edinburgh Academy when he was a pupil there in the 1970s.The 65-year-old said he was around 15 when he was initially "yanked from behind" by Colin Turner beside a school noticeboard when he was running late for class.Campbell said he was then "rag dolled" by the teacher and described being shaken, slapped and dragged across the playground.He was giving evidence during an examination of facts hearing held at Edinburgh Sheriff Court.Turner and David Bourne, another former teacher, are accused of attacking pupils at the prestigious fee-paying school but have been deemed medically unfit to stand trial.A sheriff will instead hear evidence in the case and determine whether there are grounds for a conviction.Campbell was a pupil at Edinburgh Academy between 1966 and 1978, from when he was aged five until he was 17.The BBC Radio 5 Live presenter told the court he was a "skinny teenage pupil" when he was attacked by Turner - who he said was a "physically imposing" man.Prior to the incident, he said that he and another pupil were looking at a timetable on a noticeboard after the lunchtime break, trying to find out where they should be.He said there were a few stragglers in the playground but most pupils had gone to class.Campbell told the court he was "yanked from behind", adding: "I didn't know what was going on, didn't know who it was until I turned around and he [Turner] started hitting me."He shook me around and started slapping me. He utterly lost it. It was an absolute frenzy."Teacher 'dealt with'Campbell said immediately after the incident it was as if "the red mist lifted" and he and Turner went into a nearby common room and sat down at a table. He told the court he was still sobbing.The presenter said he told the teacher "I could call the police on you for that" and that the teacher appeared "chastened."Campbell said he went home with a torn shirt. He told the court his mother saw he was "distraught" and called the school. Following this, he said there was "correspondence" and that he remembered his mother later saying that Turner had been "dealt with".Later in his evidence, Campbell told the court that he saw his Edinburgh Academy pupil file for the first time three or four weeks ago.Asked if there was any record of this incident in it, he replied: "No, it was ridiculously scant."Campbell will continue giving evidence on Thursday.

schema.headline: BBC's Nicky Campbell tells court teacher who attacked him 'completely lost it'

title: Conservatives united behind Kemi Badenoch - but party still needs to win over voters
description: It is Kemi Badenoch's Conservative Party now.Implicitly and explicitly, that was the message from the Tories' annual conference, which has wrapped up
body: It is Kemi Badenoch's Conservative Party now.Implicitly and explicitly, that was the message from the Tories' annual conference, which has wrapped up in Birmingham.It is a party very much united around her, with no murmurings of dissent about her leadership, which is quite the contrast from a year ago.The pivot point in her time as Conservative leader so far came in her address to this same gathering 12 months back, when, amid constant chatter about the prospect of Robert Jenrick seeking to topple her, she won over the party faithful with an address that oozed confidence.Not just that. Us reporters were given her speech script, allowing us to follow it line-by-line to help us report what she has said quickly and accurately. But there was a page missing towards the end. On that page was the Conservative crowd pleaser of a plan to scrap stamp duty in England and Northern Ireland.Fast forward to now and there was a familiar drill. There was plenty of chat throughout the conference and beforehand of a new policy coming on inheritance tax, and, sure enough, another page was missing towards the end of her speech with her plan on that.The plan reopens the fascinating politics and psychology of inheritance tax – which is paid by fewer than one in 20 people, external but has been described as the country's most unpopular tax, external. Why so? Advocates of cutting or scrapping it say it is because plenty aspire to one day being rich enough to end up having to pay it, plus it is a second tax on already taxed income.But the Conservatives' opponents, even before this speech, were already looking forward to the argument they anticipated after it. Reform UK, for instance, claim it is a "tax cut for multi-millionaires" and that their plan to cut income tax for millions by raising the threshold at which most people start paying it will benefit far more people.The Institute For Fiscal Studies said the "biggest beneficiaries" would be "a very well off group, external, mainly living in London and the south east of England". It also said it would "encourage wealthy people to buy (or stay in) more expensive homes in their later years". The proportion of estates subject to inheritance tax is rising rapidly, the IFS said, but forecasts are uncertain because it depends on, among other things, what happens to house prices. The Conservatives estimate their inheritance policy change would cost around £6bn a year. They claim to have identified £71bn pounds worth of cuts that can be made to government spending, including £36bn a year from benefits and welfare. The largest savings are projected to come from reforming sickness and disability benefits, where the party believes it can save £13.7bn a year, with £9.5bn a year from ending access to benefits for non-EU nationals, £4.5bn from changes to housing benefit, and £3.1bn from reintroducing the two-child limit for Universal Credit.But Work and Pensions Minister Torsten Bell said "history is very clear that promising this scale of tax cuts ends one way, external: trashing your public finances".Policy announcements aside, what stood out in this speech for me was a broader point. The veteran Conservative elections strategist Sir Lynton Crosby once suggested the party ought to "scrape the barnacles off the boat" as he put it, in reference to unpopular policies that could cause the Tories a headache during an election campaign.This speech felt like Badenoch revelling in pointing at the clean hull of the Conservative ship, what she sees as those barnacles removed, not least the high-profile defections of Jenrick and Suella Braverman.There was a striking glee and anger in her reflections about Reform UK. She sought to portray them as sleazy and pointedly decided to lean into an argument of recent months about Englishness.Braverman has argued that, given her Asian heritage, "I'm not English". "I'm proud to be British. My family and ancestors have a link to Britain which spans centuries. But in no way are we English," she wrote on social media last month, external, adding: "Englishness is an ethnicity."Badenoch expressed her personal fury at this, saying that as the mother of mixed-race children "I don't want to explain to my son, when we're watching our brilliant England team play football, that some people don't think our black players are English".The recurring message, today and over the last few days, is Badenoch cannot stand Reform and won't work with them before or after the next general election.But what she said amounted to an attack on Reform's character and the judgement of their prominent figures, rather than a significant focus on the policies we hear talked about most often by Nigel Farage.Badenoch did talk about immigration, but not at length. She largely left the issue – and the Conservative policy to withdraw from the European Convention on Human Rights, as Reform also advocates - to her shadow home secretary Chris Philp who spoke before her.Instead, Badenoch grounded this speech in the big picture tussle to be trusted between Labour and the Conservatives – and in particular who was better placed to deliver a growing economy.In tone, language and public enthusiasm for the argument, Badenoch and Andy Burnham are quite the contrast with their immediate predecessors Rishi Sunak and Sir Keir Starmer. Badenoch and Burnham both look like they are enjoying themselves on the stage, and are both enthusiastic purveyors of the core of what are their very different worldviews.Badenoch acknowledged this with what she called the "battle for the soul of this nation" in the opening minute or so of her address. It is a trailer for the debate to come this autumn and beyond.The Conservatives feel chipper and are united. But while both of these things are better than the alternative for any party leader, they are not the same as being popular.And, as Kemi Badenoch acknowledged, they are not there on that score yet, by a long chalk, with opinion polls suggesting they are more unpopular than when they were annihilated at the last general election.The numbers, for them, are dire. Just not as bad, relatively speaking, as they were.But they hope things are looking up for them: Reform has had a bruising few months, and Labour, they believe, are leaning to the Left, trying to lure Green and Liberal Democrat supporters towards them.Can the Conservatives also lure recent Lib Dem supporters in the south of England with talk of help with childcare costs whatever your income, not hiking the council tax of very expensive homes and this inheritance tax plan?This, Tories hope, there are now gaps in the political market they can exploit.They crave catching and overtaking Reform in the polls, in the hope that after that there is a tipping point allowing them to credibly claim they are the most viable alternative to a Labour or Labour-led future government. Let's see.

schema.headline: Conservatives united behind Kemi Badenoch - but party still needs to win over voters

title: Children killed while they slept as Russian missile kills 19 in block of flats
description: A Russian missile has killed 19 people including five children in an apartment block in northern Ukraine, destroying 30 flats as families slept.Three
body: A Russian missile has killed 19 people including five children in an apartment block in northern Ukraine, destroying 30 flats as families slept.Three of the children were one-year-olds in the attack on Pryluky, east of Kyiv, early on Wednesday, and one of the boys died with his mother and grandmother, officials said.Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky said it was one of Russia's "most vile strikes", and suggested the Russian military had carried it out as a "birthday gift" to Vladimir Putin, who turned 74 on Wednesday.Moscow made no mention of the attack on Pryluky but said its "massive strike" had targeted military industries in Kyiv and elsewhere.Across the country, the death toll on Wednesday climbed to 25, as Russian strikes claimed two lives in the capital, two in Kremenchuk, and two more in Oleksandriya. More than 430 apartments and private homes were damaged and dozens of people were injured in the attack on the central city of Kremenchuk, the regional leader said.Rescue teams in Pryluky spent hours searching for victims in the rubble of a five-storey block of flats.Late in the afternoon rescuers said the body of a fifth child had been found at the scene. More than 50 residents were wounded in the attack that also damaged other residential buildings as well as a youth centre.Chernihiv regional head Vyacheslav Chaus said the town was hit by five cruise missiles, one of which slammed into the apartment building.Zelensky named the one-year-old victims as Oleksandr, Kyrylo, and Serhii, and said a boy of eight called Maxsym had also been killed.Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said a boy called Sasha had died with his mother, Kateryna and her mother Viktoriia, and only the boy's elder sister Olha had survived. Local reports said they had lived on the fifth floor and that Viktoriia had been looking after her grandson while her daughter worked in a factory.Ukraine's air force said it had succeeded in shooting down five ballistic missiles and 39 cruise missiles and more than 100 drones, including 46 of Russia's jet-powered drones which have caused so much damage in recent weeks.However, that would mean that as many as 26 cruise or ballistic missiles penetrated its defences, and Zelensky renewed a call for allies to provide air defence support packages to Ukraine.According to Zelensky, one of the "key targets" of the attack was Ukraine's energy infrastructure, which Moscow earlier said it would intensify strikes on following Ukraine's strikes on Moscow's energy facilities.In a separate post on Wednesday, Zelensky said Ukraine had struck four targets in retaliatory attacks in the past 24 hours, including two oil facilities and a training ground as well as a target in the Black Sea.On Tuesday evening, footage emerged showing a huge plume of smoke engulfing an oil tanker off the coast of Sochi, along the Black Sea in southern Russia.The Russian transport ministry later said unmanned boats had attacked the Liberian-flagged Aframax Rio oil tanker. Authorities claim the crew was rescued.Separately, Bulgaria has halted a search for the missing crew of a ship that sank after being hit by a drone on Tuesday, Vice-Admiral Rumen Nikolov from the Maritime Administration Executive Agency said, as reported by Bulgaria's BTA news agency. No details of the crew are known, but Nikolov said it was assumed there were Syrians on board.Tracking data shows the ship was anchored at the southern end of the Bosphorus strait until Monday when it entered the Black Sea heading north. Its last reported position on ship-tracking site MarineTraffic was at 23:43 GMT on Monday in what is known as the Bulgarian exclusive economic zone of the Black Sea.Bulgarian specialist news outlet Maritime.bg reported the Alfa Watan was attacked by a drone and sank 70nm (130km) east of Byala.As well as the civilian cargo ship, a second vessel - carrying grain - was also hit within Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone, its Prime Minister Rumen Radev said on Tuesday. The 18 crew members on the second vessel were rescued.Bulgaria has not said who it believes was behind the attacks, and Moscow has not commented on the incident.Russia has intensified strikes in the Black Sea, particularly the eastern side, as part of its war against Ukraine. In an evening address on Tuesday, Zelensky claimed Russia was responsible for the attacks.Additional reporting by BBC Verify

schema.headline: Children killed while they slept as Russian missile kills 19 in block of flats

title: Boots sold in £7bn deal to Canadian billionaire family
description: Boots, the High Street pharmacy and retail chain, has been sold in an $8.9bn (£6.7bn) deal to Canada's billionaire Weston family.Wittington Investment
body: Boots, the High Street pharmacy and retail chain, has been sold in an $8.9bn (£6.7bn) deal to Canada's billionaire Weston family.Wittington Investments, the holding company, confirmed it had agreed to buy the 177-year-old retailer on Wednesday from US private equity firm Sycamore Partners and the Pessina family.Boots started as a simple apothecary in Nottingham but has evolved to become a stalwart of the High Street, expanding its business to sell a vast range of health and beauty products, meal deals and travel accessories.The chain has performed well in recent years despite challenges from rivals and changing shopping habits.Its stores have seen lower footfall as people switched to working from home rather than visiting town and city centre offices every weekday.It has closed hundreds of branches across the UK in recent years, leaving it with about 1,800 stores and 51,000 employees, but remains a familiar British brand.In its most recent annual results, Boots generated £7.5bn in sales - a 3.2% increase on 2024. Retail expert Catherine Shuttleworth, chief executive of savvy marketing, said shoppers were unlikely to see much change to stores in the coming months, but added what they can "expect over time is an improved shopping experience as the new owners invest in the business".She said health and beauty was a "massive area for growth", and fresh investment from its new ownership would help. The last two decades has seen several changes of ownership under discussion and sometimes completed.Sycamore only owned the retailer for 18 months, and Shuttleworth said the chopping and changing of owners had been "an unhelpful distraction".The company was established by John Boot, who opened the first herbalist store in Nottingham, offering an affordable alternative to traditional medicines in 1849.It has since expanded over the decades into selling various products, but health products have remained a key part of its business. As well as vaccines, it offers eye and hearing tests, providing much needed health care support in everyday moments as well as at times of national crisis like the coronavirus pandemic. It launched its loyalty scheme in 1997, the Advantage Card, which became hugely popular and a move repeated by various retailers since.Galen Weston, the chairman of Wittington, will become chairman of Boots.He signalled the new owners had fresh plans for the chain, including shop upgrades and an expansion of healthcare services."We see a meaningful opportunity to make a great business even better through stable long-term ownership, further capital investment, and the renewed operating focus required to serve customers with excellence for generations to come," he said.The Weston family will be buying Boots' retail operations in the UK and Ireland, Boots Opticians, No7 Beauty Company and its Thailand and franchised businesses. It is set be completed in early 2027.The Weston family owns the Canadian grocery chain Loblaws, pharmacy business Shoppers Drug Mart, and previously owned the London department store Selfridges from 2003 to 2021, before selling it for $4bn.The separate UK branch of the Weston family is the majority owner of Associated British Foods, the parent firm of Primark.The Westons were ranked fifth on this year's Sunday Times Rich List with a combined fortune of almost £19bn.Wittington will have operational control over Boots, it has secured ownership in partnership with Fairfax Financial Holdings, a Toronto-based holding company.Sycamore Partners, in partnership with Stefano Pessina and his family, will retain ownership of The Boots Group's Farmacias Benavides in Mexico and Alliance Healthcare Deutschland in Germany.

schema.headline: Boots sold in £7bn deal to Canadian billionaire family

title: Fifa: Ex-Spurs player Ramon Vega intends to stand in 2027 presidential election
description: Former Tottenham Hotspur defender Ramon Vega says he intends to stand as a candidate in next year's Fifa presidential election.The 55-year-old is the
body: Former Tottenham Hotspur defender Ramon Vega says he intends to stand as a candidate in next year's Fifa presidential election.The 55-year-old is the first person to confirm they want to challenge Gianni Infantino, who has defied calls to step down in the wake of his failed plan to sell off stakes in the World Cup to private investors, which has sparked a major backlash across football.A former Switzerland centre-back, Vega also played for Celtic and Watford and has worked in finance since retiring from football in 2004."I am standing to reunite the global football family, deliver genuine and lasting reform, modernise Fifa for the 21st Century, restore stability and credibility, and rebuild the trust that our game urgently needs," he said.Meanwhile, Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa - president of the Asian Football Confederation - has written to Infantino, distancing himself from an external review of Fifa's governance system.In his letter - seen by BBC Sport - Sheikh Salman proposes that Fifa's council sets up a working group to examine potential reforms, "rather than being outsourced to an external party".Last month, Infantino said he was "fully committed to leading Fifa" despite Uefa, Concacaf and the Asian Football Confederation calling for him to quit.Vega considered running for Fifa's top job in 2015 following the suspension of former president Sepp Blatter.Four years later he said he would stand against Infantino, but failed to garner enough support to be included in the ballot, having required the backing of five of Fifa's 211 member federations. Candidates must also be proposed by a member association and have played an active role in the game for two of the past five years, as well as passing an eligibility check by a review committee. "I am standing because my life has prepared me to serve the game," Vega said in a statement announcing his candidacy."Football does not belong to presidents, confederations or administrators. Football is greater than any position, any individual or any institution."It is the people's game and belongs to everyone: the players, coaches, referees, supporters, volunteers, clubs, leagues, associations and communities that give football its life."It belongs to every child discovering the game, every professional carrying the hopes of a nation, and the billions of supporters whose passion makes football the world's game."Football must always come first. Yet for too long, division has fractured our football family."The current leadership has demoralised the game. Weak governance has damaged Fifa's credibility and eroded trust across the global football family. We must stop this conflict from escalating."Ego-driven battles within football administration must never be allowed to damage those who matter most: the players, coaches, referees and supporters around the world. They are not responsible for these conflicts. They deserve better."Vega concluded: "Football is in the emergency room, on life support. We cannot wait any longer. Fifa needs a new direction and fundamental reform."We must reunite the football family, restore trust, bring stability and modernise Fifa's governance. This requires decisive change - not cosmetic adjustments."It comes with Sheikh Salman appearing to soften his stance towards Infantino just two months after the AFC president signed a joint letter with the heads of Uefa and Concacaf accusing the Fifa president of breaking trust "through deception" over his Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) plan.At the time, the three confederations said any review of Fifa's governance must be "conducted by a fully independent third party".Now, however, Salman says he believes the process should be "driven by the football institutions themselves, rather than being outsourced to an external party".He added: "I believe there is value in taking this opportunity to consider constructively whether Fifa's existing governance arrangements can be strengthened."The issue is not necessarily whether this requires a wholesale redesign of Fifa's governance system."Fifa's council meets in Zurich next week for the first time since the FFE plan emerged in July.

schema.headline: Fifa: Ex-Spurs player Ramon Vega intends to stand in 2027 presidential election

title: Notorious Glasgow gangland enforcer Paul Ferris dies aged 62
description: Image source, Garry F McHargImage caption, Ferris turned to writing about his life in Glasgow's underworldByPaul O'HareBBC Scotland and Benjamin Russe
body: Image source, Garry F McHargImage caption, Ferris turned to writing about his life in Glasgow's underworldByPaul O'HareBBC Scotland and Benjamin Russell BBC ScotlandUpdated 5 hours agoA Glasgow gangland enforcer who wrote books about his underworld experiences has died at the age of 62. Paul Ferris is believed to have died on Tuesday night at the city's Queen Elizabeth University Hospital after a short illness. He was cleared of the murder of crime boss Arthur Thompson's son, Arthur Thompson Jnr, in 1992, before being jailed for seven years in 1998 for gun-running.His first book, The Ferris Conspiracy, was published in 2001.It was later made into a 2013 film, The Wee Man, featuring Line of Duty star Martin Compston as Ferris.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Ferris left prison in 2002 after completing a seven-year sentencePhotographer Brian Anderson, who first met Ferris for a newspaper assignment in 2002, broke the news of his death on his Naked City Facebook page.Describing Ferris as a best-selling author and a "former notorious criminal", he wrote: "News of his death will come as a shock to many who knew him throughout the different chapters of his life."Anderson later told BBC Scotland News: "We got on really well. I found him polite, funny and kind."It was a shock to everyone that I remained friends with Paul for 25 years."Thompson, who had links to the Krays in London, was an old school Glasgow criminal known as The Godfather.By the early 80s, Ferris had become part of his gang as an enforcer, someone who threatened and, when necessary, meted out violence. He rapidly built a fearsome reputation that extended beyond the city.But their relationship took a remarkable twist in August 1991 when Arthur "Fat Boy" Thompson Jnr, was shot dead outside the family's Provanmill home.It was named The Ponderosa after the ranch in the hit US Western television series, Bonanza.Ferris was arrested as the prime suspect in Thompson Jnr's murder but two others were also incriminated. His friends Joe "Bananas" Hanlon and Bobby Glover did not live to stand trial.On the day of Thompson Jnr's funeral both men were found shot dead in a car on the cortege route.The murders remain unsolved.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, The Wee Man, a film based on his life, was released in 2013The following year Ferris's trial became, at the time, the longest and most expensive criminal case in Scottish legal history. More than 300 witnesses gave evidence during the 54-day proceedings, which were estimated to have cost £4m.The prosecution case relied heavily on the evidence of Dennis Woodman, who claimed Ferris had confessed to the killing while both men were being held in Barlinnie Prison. Defence lawyers challenged the credibility of the evidence and argued the case against Ferris was deeply flawed. After more than 24 hours of deliberations, the jury acquitted Ferris of murder and all other charges in 1992.No-one has ever been convicted of Thompson Jnr's killing.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Donald Findlay KC represented Ferris during the murder trialIn 2020 Donald Findlay KC - who defended Ferris in court - told Hey Legal, external that the case had been the most memorable of his career.He said: "The trial of Paul Ferris for the murder of Arthur Thompson Jr had virtually all the great characters of Glasgow in that trial one way or another."Young Arthur was dead, his father was a witness, Ferris was regarded by the police as the heir apparent to Arthur Thompson Sr."We had supergrasses, it just had everything that was going for it."I forget how many charges that there were but of course Ferris walked on each and every one of them."Following his release from prison in 2002 after being jailed on gun-running charges, Ferris turned to writing.His debut book was made into a movie which starred Martin Compston - who had found fame as a teenager in Ken Loach's Sweet Sixteen - as Ferris.John Hannah played his arch rival, Tam "The Licensee" McGraw.The crime boss, who died in 2007 aged 55, had been linked to crimes ranging from drug smuggling to murder for more than three decades.The movie was shot in London due to problems securing permission from Glasgow City Council and the police to film in Ferris's home city.Image caption, Former Scottish Crime and Drug Enforcement Agency director general Graeme Pearson first met Ferris when the convicted gun-runner was a teenagerFerris went on to publish two further books, Vendetta and Villains, with crime writer Reg McKay, who died in 2012.Graeme Pearson, former director general of the Scottish Crime and Drug Enforcement Agency, first encountered the convicted gun-runner when he was a teenager.Pearson told BBC Scotland News that Ferris went on to develop a fearsome reputation.He said: "Certainly, in his active days, he wouldn't be a man that you would choose to go to dinner with."The ex-Labour MSP added: "At one stage in his life he was a very dangerous character."He was someone who seemed to take pleasure in his reputation for violence."Having said that, I think that in later life he certainly seemed to outlive that reputation and would appear to have put that whole gangster profile behind him."

schema.headline: Notorious Glasgow gangland enforcer Paul Ferris dies aged 62

title: Israelis demand accountability over 7 October failures three years after attacks
description: Image source, ReutersImage caption, Residents of Kfar Aza attended a memorial ceremony on Wednesday for those killed on 7 October 2023ByLucy Williamso
body: Image source, ReutersImage caption, Residents of Kfar Aza attended a memorial ceremony on Wednesday for those killed on 7 October 2023ByLucy WilliamsonMiddle East correspondentReporting fromJerusalem and Kfar AzaAs the sky began to lighten over Israel's border with Gaza on Wednesday, the people of Kfar Aza moved silently towards the armoury at the centre of the kibbutz.It was there, shortly after 07:00 on 7 October 2023, that Hamas-led attackers killed half the community's 14-member civil defence squad. They were among 64 killed and 19 kidnapped from the community that day.The pain of those attacks is still fresh here. But three years on, there are questions about who else should pay the price for Israel's security failure."I need my country to take responsibility," said Inbar Goldstein, whose brother and niece were killed, and four other relatives kidnapped from Kfar Aza.The 7 October attack was the deadliest Israel had suffered since its creation in 1948. About 1,200 people were killed across southern Israel by gunmen who broke through the border fence and attacked communities there. Another 251 people were taken back to Gaza as hostages.Three years on from Israel's biggest security failure, there is still no independent state inquiry into how it was allowed to happen.And the man in charge at the time of that failure - Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu - is running for election again, with the same campaign promise: to be stronger and tougher than anyone else in protecting Israel from its enemies."Nobody investigated the roots [of the attack]. It didn't start or end on October 7th - it's a long process of abandonment," Goldstein said.Image source, ReutersImage caption, More than 60 residents of Kfar Aza were killed by Hamas-led gunmen and 19 were taken hostage three years agoAside from Hamas's responsibility for the attack itself, there are growing questions in Israel around what caused the country's intelligence failure, what information was passed to military and political leaders in the run-up to the attacks, and what Netanyahu himself knew.For months beforehand, young female soldiers posted at bases along the Gaza border to watch for suspicious activity had warned their superiors about possible preparations for an attack.Among them was Roni Eshel. She was killed with 14 other members of her unit when gunmen overran their base at Nahal Oz, just next to Kfar Aza."There are so many questions," her uncle Elad Levy told me. "Were the Egyptians warning the prime minister? The Emiratis? Were there no other warnings Netanyahu ignored?  We need to find out what happened – not just on the day, but the year before, and five years before that.""The truth should be clear," he continued. "If we don't inquire into this, it will happen again and again."Image source, EPAImage caption, Benjamin Netanyahu has rejected any personal responsibility for security failures three years agoOver the past three years, there have been mounting reports of warnings being given to Netanyahu - by his own security chief, as well as by regional neighbours – which he denies.Last month, Israel's Haaretz newspaper published extracts from a new book, alleging that the leader of the United Arab Emirates had called Netanyahu 10 days before the attack to warn of Hamas plans for a major operation.Netanyahu's office has dismissed the report as "an absolute lie" and has said he will sue the newspaper.Amir Ohana, a member of Netanyahu's Likud party, said in a social media video last month that it was "preposterous and absurd" to suggest that Netanyahu could have known about the attack when the former Hamas leader in Gaza, Yahya Sinwar, had only told a handful of people.Israel's prime minister, he said, had since reshaped the Middle East and did not give up, "even when voices inside and outside Israel called on him to stop".Netanyahu has blamed his own security chiefs for the failures that led to the 7 October attacks, accusing them of deliberately choosing not to wake him in the hours beforehand, for fear that he would order a massive deployment of the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) and escalate the situation."God forbid we wake up the prime minister and he says, 'Wake up the entire IDF immediately, scramble the air force!'" he told Israel's right-wing Channel 14 television network."What would have happened if they had woken me? This would not have happened," he said, suggesting that his response would have better protected Israel from the attacks.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Netanyahu denied reports that he was warned by the UAE's president days before Hamas attackedYaakov Katz, a journalist and author of several books on Israel's defence, has written about the growing concerns over Hamas activity that emerged in the hours leading up to the assault.In his book, While Israel Slept, he describes calls between senior military figures and intelligence chiefs in the early hours of the morning, the sudden recall of commanders from leave, and the dispatch of an elite intelligence unit to the border.He told me their expectation was, at worst, a small, limited incursion by Hamas fighters."So why would [Netanyahu] order a massive pre-emptive strike by the IDF, if every security chief is telling him this is not what this is going to be? Waking him would not have made a difference."But he said Netanyahu faced other questions about his failure to spot what was happening."You were the prime minister, you set the policy," he said. "You created a doctrine and a policy of containment that trickled down to the last soldier manning the watchtower on the border with Gaza: contain Hamas, separate the Palestinians, and keep Hamas in power to prevent the establishment of a Palestinian state."Image source, ReutersImage caption, Israelis have held protests to demand the establishment of a state commission of inquiryFor years, Netanyahu oversaw a policy of containing - not confronting - Hamas in Gaza, during which Israeli governments allowed Qatar to provide hundreds of millions of dollars of aid for Gaza.A month after the 7 October attacks, he told a German newspaper that claims he wanted to strengthen Hamas were "an absolute lie"."On the contrary we wanted to continue to weaken Hamas as much as we could," he told Die Welt. "But the money was meant to avoid a civilian catastrophe - that is the only reason."Months after the attack, the IDF's then-chief of staff, Lt Gen Herzi Halevi, publicly apologised for the failure to defend civilians, saying he carried that weight on his shoulders and in his heart.He resigned. A raft of military commanders were later fired, and Israel's domestic intelligence chief left his position.Netanyahu has so far rejected any personal responsibility for the attacks.Col Richard Hecht was the IDF's international spokesman on 7 October. He told me the refusal of political leaders - including Netanyahu - to accept responsibility was part of the reason he resigned six months later."It's a disgrace," he told me. "When you look at accountability, within the IDF I don't think there's a problem. And that's the pain. That's one of the main causes of bad blood between the political echelon and the military."At a memorial ceremony in Jerusalem on Monday, the father of one of those killed on 7 October stood up to challenge the prime minister."You didn't protect my son, you didn't protect all those who were murdered," he said, before security guards led him away. "Shame! Disgrace!"Image source, EPAImage caption, "Netanyahu does not surrender" is a slogan of his right-wing Likud partyThree years on from the attacks, calls for accountability are growing. Campaigners have asked Israel's highest court to force the government into establishing a state commission of inquiry.Yizhar Shai, a former minister and opposition politician whose youngest son Yaron, a soldier, was killed on 7 October, is part of that campaign."We are going into these elections almost blindfolded as it relates to October 7th," he told me during a protest in Tel Aviv last week. "Our prime minister has never given a detailed, thorough explanation under oath, where he would be asked all the tough questions and have to explain everything."Netanyahu has consistently refused a state inquiry led by Israel's Supreme Court, arguing recently that the country's judiciary would be biased against him.Before calling an election, his government proposed an alternative "national commission of inquiry", whose members would be appointed by political parties.But despite passing a raft of other legislation before parliament ended its session in July, Israel's government said it ran out of time to pass a bill setting out its plans for the inquiry.We approached several members of his Likud party for an interview, without success. We also requested that the party respond to their critics, and are waiting for their response.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Gadi Eisenkot and other opposition leaders have backed calls for a state commission of inquiryNetanyahu's denial of responsibility has now become an election issue, as he prepares to run for re-election later this month.A video game called Sleepy Bibi, released by the team of his main opponent, Gadi Eisenkot, asks players to help the prime minister avoid responsibility by dodging warnings of an attack and "making it to bed safely".Netanyahu has styled himself for decades as Israel's "Mr Security", and despite presiding over the worst security failure in Israel's history, is running on the same security platform again.For the past three years, he focused on waging new wars against Israel's enemies - Hamas, Hezbollah and Iran.Polls suggest a close race, and that the 7 October attacks are central to many voters' decisions.Yaakov Katz says the legacy of 7 October is a coin with two sides."There are the failures, the mistakes that led to the Hamas invasion," he told me. "But there's the other side, which is Netanyahu's argument; that [he] has re-engineered the Middle East and made Israel a safer place today. And that is an argument Israelis take with them to the polls."The shadow of the attacks hangs over this election, dividing Israel once again along political lines.For supporters, it confirms that Benjamin Netanyahu is still needed to keep Israel safe.Critics say his political survival puts Israel at risk.

schema.headline: Israelis demand accountability over 7 October failures three years after attacks

title: Fraudster jailed over multi-million pound PPE scam
description: A fraudster has been jailed for helping to scam medical companies out of millions of pounds through bogus personal protective equipment (PPE) deals du
body: A fraudster has been jailed for helping to scam medical companies out of millions of pounds through bogus personal protective equipment (PPE) deals during the Covid-19 pandemic.Craig Morris, 43, and Jogesh Bhandari, 60, bought luxury cars, holidays and a new home after pretending they could supply millions of boxes of nitrile gloves in the US and Germany. They were convicted of two counts of conspiracy to commit fraud by false representation as well as concealing and transferring criminal property at Leicester Crown Court in July.On Wednesday, Morris received three years and nine months in prison. Jogesh, of Mitchell Drive, Loughborough, Leicestershire, will be sentenced later.Jogesh told his counsel he was taking a "very extreme painkiller" after having a pacemaker fitted last week and was not able to travel to Northampton, where the sentencing hearing took place.His wife, former pharmacist Meenakashi Bhandari, 58, also of Mitchell Drive, did attend the sentencing hearing.She was found guilty of concealing and transferring criminal property. She was given a two-year prison sentence, suspended for two years, 250 hours of unpaid work and 15 days of rehabilitation activity.Judge William Harbage KC said there was "no medical evidence" to properly explain Jogesh's absence and said a bench warrant would be issued. He is expected to be sentenced on 16 October.Prosecutor Michael Bisgrove told the court Jogesh was the "driving force and the instigator" of the offending, while Morris, of Forest Drive in Lytham St Annes, Lancashire, was "very much working for him".He said: "The offences took place during the Covid-19 pandemic at a time when there was a desperate shortage of personal protective equipment (PPE)."In that shortage, the offenders, particularly Mr Bhandari and Mr Morris, saw the opportunity to make money by fraud."The court heard that Jogesh and Morris made fraudulent deals under a company called Banton."They pretended to be big players in the PPE market. They pretended to have PPE for sale and to be able to buy vast amounts of it," Bisgrove added.The court heard they defrauded US company Med18 and German firm MedTech by sending contracts for equipment they did not have.Bisgrove said: "In the course of the fraud, they took millions of pounds which they used for their own benefit to buy cars, luxury goods and property."

schema.headline: Fraudster jailed over multi-million pound PPE scam

title: Israelis mourn 7 October attack victims as Gaza lies in ruins three years on
description: Crowds also filed into the small cemetery at Kibbutz Kfar Aza, where 64 residents were killed and 19 were taken hostage on 7 October.Zion Regev, a com
body: Crowds also filed into the small cemetery at Kibbutz Kfar Aza, where 64 residents were killed and 19 were taken hostage on 7 October.Zion Regev, a community leader, said most surviving residents had yet to return to their homes because of the trauma of what happened."This is the first time we are doing all the things here in the kibbutz," he told Reuters news agency. "It's a very emotional day, it's a very difficult day for our community, three years after 7 October."A man who reportedly helped to fend off Hamas attackers at Kibbutz Magen praised IDF troops who "fought so bravely" during the raid.Speaking to crowds at the national memorial event at Tel Aviv's Yarkon Park on Wednesday evening, Ido Yakir said Israel would remember everyone "who knew that they had to give their lives in order to save others".In a statement released by his office on Wednesday afternoon, Netanyahu said he had lit a memorial candle commemorating every victim of 7 October."We will complete the mission: we have settled the score and will continue settling the score with all the murderers," he added.At a ceremony on Monday marking the Jewish calendar's anniversary of the attack, the prime minister said Israel had killed 4,000 out of the 6,000 Palestinians who infiltrated Israel from Gaza that day.In Tel Aviv's Dizengoff Square, Israeli anti-government protesters dyed the fountain red to mark the anniversary of the attack.The fountain has been used as a memorial site for those killed, with pictures, flowers and messages laid around the basin wall.Protesters also briefly blocked one of the main highways in the city to hold a moment of silence on Wednesday morning.They held banners that read, "the people will remember their sons and daughters", along with others that said "a complete failure" and "guilty" next to an image of Netanyahu.Many senior Israeli defence and security officials have resigned or been fired since the attack took place. But there has not been an independent commission of inquiry into Israel's worst security failure.The prime minister has rejected any personal responsibility and has refused to establish a state inquiry led by Israel's Supreme Court, arguing recently that the country's judiciary would be biased against him.Einav Zangauker became an outspoken critic of the Netanyahu government while her son, Matan, was in captivity in Gaza. He was released last October as part of the ceasefire agreement."They're trying to make us forget what happened on 7 October," she told Army Radio. "We won't forget, we will demand the truth."Memorial events were organised in other countries around the world, including in Germany, where the Jewish students' union held a vigil at Berlin's Brandenburg Gate.German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said the Hamas-led attack marked a "profound rupture". "We commemorate the victims, we share their pain," he said, adding that antisemitism must be confronted with "even greater resolve".UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham told Britain's Jewish community: "We stand with you.""The impact of the attacks has been felt not just in Israel, but in Jewish communities across the world who still bear the burden of the tragic events that day," he said.Outside Downing Street, a vigil was also held to commemorate British-Israelis killed in the initial attack, later as hostages, or in fighting with Hamas.Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission, said: "The unspeakable savagery and terror of 7 October must never happen again."She also said that the European Union "remains ready to help turn today's fragile ceasefire into a durable peace, based on a two-state solution."Speaking to reporters outside the White House on Wednesday, US President Donald Trump said he had spoken to Netanyahu and wished the people of Israel well."That was a horrible day, a horrible tragedy," he said.This is the first anniversary of the 7 October attack with no hostages remaining in Gaza, but a US-brokered ceasefire deal from last year has failed to deliver peace or bring security. There has been no end to Gaza's deadliest ever war, as Israel continues to carry out near-daily attacks. More than 1,460 people have been killed there since the ceasefire took effect, according to Gaza health ministry. The Israeli military says at least seven Israeli soldiers have been killed in the strip over the same period.Most of Gaza is in ruins, with nearly all the 2.1 million population still displaced amid dire humanitarian conditions. An estimated 80% of all structures have been destroyed or damaged during the war, leaving more than 60 million tonnes of rubble piled up and 1.2 million people living in tents or shelters, according to the UN.Families who have been displaced several times during the war increasingly ask where they could go next, and whether they might even be forced to leave Gaza altogether.Mohammed Emad al-Din, a 38-year-old father of two who works as a barber in Gaza City, said he had been displaced five times. His home was destroyed and his barber shop was partially damaged. He told the BBC that the fear of being forced out of Gaza now follows him even into his dreams."I don't believe Israel caused all this destruction for nothing," he said. "They have turned Gaza into a place that is almost impossible to live in, and I fear that we will eventually end up outside the place where we were born."Another displaced Palestinian, Atta Saeed Hassan Shweikh, told the BBC that his son, daughter, sister and her children had all been killed during the war.Speaking from Gaza City, he said Palestinians were "living in graves while still alive" and have endured "severe suffering".At least three Palestinians were killed in Israeli strikes in the northern town of Beit Lahia and the southern city of Khan Younis on Wednesday, medics said.The Israeli military said it struck two Hamas operatives in northern Gaza overnight, one of whom it accused of planting explosives near the so-called Yellow Line, which marks the territory still occupied by Israeli forces.Hamas - which is proscribed as a terrorist organisation by Israel, the UK and others - released a statement  praising the 7 October attack as a "historic milestone" in its "ongoing struggle project".The statement, attributed to the group and disseminated in Palestinian media, called the attack "a natural response" to "bitter suffering" imposed by Israel.

schema.headline: Israelis mourn 7 October attack victims as Gaza lies in ruins three years on

title: Premier League: How settled is the table already?
description: Is it too early to look at Premier League table?Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Arsenal are chasing back-to-back Premier League titlesByChris
body: Is it too early to look at Premier League table?Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Arsenal are chasing back-to-back Premier League titlesByChris CollinsonBBC Sport statisticianJust five games in, it might seem a bit early to pay much attention to the Premier League table - but it's probably more settled than you think.While it would be no surprise if Manchester City and Arsenal finish as the top two - outside of any points deductions or sanctions directed City's way - will Brentford really qualify for Europe, Hull stay up and Tottenham be involved in yet another relegation battle? Recent history certainly suggests it is likely.It has to be mentioned there is a huge asterisk hanging over the Premier League table at the moment after Manchester City were found guilty of the majority of the Premier League charges levelled at them.The Premier League leaders have appealed but, if the guilty verdict remains, potential sanctions could have a significant impact on the table. Until then, we can only deal with the table as it is now.If we look at the Premier League after five games last season and where teams ultimately ended up, the final table was already starting to take shape as 13 of the 20 sides finished within four places of where they sat even at this early stage (65%).Eventual champions Arsenal were second, Sunderland were already seventh ahead of finishing there eight months later, and two of the three sides that were relegated were already in the bottom three.There were some notable exceptions. Aston Villa and Tottenham effectively swapped places at either end of the table, with Villa rising from the bottom three to finish in the top four and Spurs dropping to 17th.It is a similar story across the last 10 seasons of the Premier League. More than two-thirds of teams finished within four places of where they were after five games (138 out of 200), with 27 of those sitting in exactly the same position 33 games later.Another 50 teams finished between five and nine places from where they were at this stage, meaning that just 12 teams in the past decade moved up or down the table by double digits after this point, with three of those coming last season.However, one part of the table that does not settle quickly is the top spot. The side leading the Premier League after five games has gone on to win the title in just one of the past six seasons - Manchester City doing so in 2023-24 - and just three times in the past 11 seasons.Even the fact that Manchester City have five wins out of five so far does not mean much. They also won their first five games under Manuel Pellegrini in 2015-16 and in Pep Guardiola's first season in 2016-17 but did not go on to win the title on either occasion (although they did in 2023-24).Chelsea in 2018-19, Arsenal in 2022-23 and Liverpool last season were also top with a 100% record at this stage but had little to show for it at the end of the season.However, the eventual champions have been in the top two at this point in each of the last four campaigns, suggesting - potential punishments aside - it will be Manchester City or Arsenal that lifts the trophy. The last team to be outside the top two after five games and win the title were Manchester City in 2021-22, who were fifth with just 10 points.The top end of the table overall has sometimes settled surprisingly quickly in recent years. The top eight after five games in 2024-25 finished as the top eight at the end of that season (although not in the same order), while the top six in 2019-20 and top seven in 2016-17 were also in place at this early stage.While being top after five games has not meant much in recent seasons, being bottom certainly has.After finishing just one place above the drop in the last two campaigns, Tottenham could well be in trouble once again as the side bottom of the Premier League after five games has been relegated in six of the past seven seasons.Being bottom this early did not used to be such a bad omen. Between 2013-14 and 2018-19, only one of the six sides that were propping up the table after five games ended up going down - Newcastle in 2015-16 - while Crystal Palace finished as high as 11th in 2017-18.In fact, the good news for Tottenham fans is that the last time they were in this situation, they finished eighth. The club were bottom with just two points after five games in 2008-09 but, after replacing manager Juande Ramos with Harry Redknapp three games later, still finished in the top half.Looking at the relegation battle more broadly, at least one of the teams in the bottom three at this stage has been relegated in the last eight seasons - so one of Tottenham, Fulham and Coventry will very likely be heading to the Championship in May.The pool of contestants for this season's relegation battle may already be decided too as the three sides that ultimately went down in the past three seasons were all in the bottom six after five games, which would add Bournemouth, Aston Villa and Crystal Palace to the mix.The last sides to be outside the bottom six at this point but relegated were Leeds and Southampton in 2022-23, who were both in the top half (7th and 9th). With their teams currently sat in 8th and 11th place, Hull and Ipswich fans will hope that is still the case at the end of this campaign.While the season may well have barely begun, the Premier League table is already starting to take shape.

schema.headline: Premier League: How settled is the table already?
